questions.case_context: Sister Mary Fernandez, Principal of a convent school in Agartala, filed a defamation case against Ali Kehtan and John Augustine who submitted a complaint to the Deputy Commissioner alleging the school building was unsafe, it was a money-minting institution, there was indiscipline, and the school had become a meeting place for both sexes. The SDM found the allegations false and dismissed the complaint. A criminal defamation case was registered. The accused applied for anticipatory bail. Sister Mary also filed a civil suit for compensation.

sub_questions.question_text: What is criminal defamation in Indian law?

key_points: Section 499 of IPC 1860 defines defamation

Making or publishing any imputation concerning any person by words (spoken or intended to be read), signs, or visible representations, intending to harm or knowing it will harm the reputation of that person
Explanation 1: Imputation to a deceased person can amount to defamation if it would harm their reputation if living and is intended to hurt the feelings of their family
Explanation 2: Imputation concerning a company or association can amount to defamation
Explanation 3: Imputation in the form of alternative or expressed ironically may amount to defamation

Explanation 4: Imputation harms reputation only if it lowers moral or intellectual character, lowers character in respect of caste or calling, lowers credit, or causes belief that the body is in a loathsome or disgraceful state
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Under Section 499 IPC, whoever by words (spoken or to be read), signs, or visible representations makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing/having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of that person, is said to defame that person. Four explanations clarify scope: includes deceased persons (if hurtful to family), companies/associations, ironic imputations, and an imputation harms reputation if it lowers moral/intellectual character, caste/calling character, credit, or causes belief the body is in a loathsome state.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites Section 499 IPC with all 4 explanations explained correctly
evaluation_criteria.good: Cites Section 499 IPC with at least 2-3 explanations
evaluation_criteria.partial: Defines defamation in own words without citing the provision or missing explanations
evaluation_criteria.minimal: Only a vague definition without legal backing

sub_questions.question_text: Is the application for 'anticipatory bail' by accused Ali Kehtan and John Augustine maintainable? Explain.

key_points: Section 438 of CrPC 1973 governs anticipatory bail
Anticipatory bail is available when a person has reason to believe they may be arrested on accusation of a NON-BAILABLE offence
Application can be made to High Court or Court of Session
Defamation is a BAILABLE offence
Since defamation is bailable, anticipatory bail application is NOT maintainable
Conclusion: Application of Ali Kehtan and John Augustine is non-maintainable
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Section 438 CrPC provides for anticipatory bail only when a person apprehends arrest for a NON-BAILABLE offence. Since defamation is a bailable offence, the accused cannot apply for anticipatory bail. Therefore, the application of Ali Kehtan and John Augustine is non-maintainable.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites Section 438 CrPC, correctly identifies defamation as bailable, and concludes application is non-maintainable
evaluation_criteria.good: Correctly concludes non-maintainability with correct reason even without specific section citation
evaluation_criteria.partial: Mentions anticipatory bail concept but unclear on bailable/non-bailable distinction

sub_questions.question_text: Whether the complaint filed by Ali Kehtan and John Augustine against Sister Mary Fernandez leads to Libel defamation or Slander defamation? Explain.

key_points: Libel: Defamatory statement in permanent and visible form – written words, caricatures, cinema films, effigy, statue, recorded words, printing or pictures
Slander: Defamatory statement made with spoken words or transitory form – gestures, spoken words, inarticulate sounds
The complaint was a WRITTEN document submitted to the Deputy Commissioner
Conclusion: It constitutes LIBEL defamation
Alternate answer: Section 499 IPC 8th exception – complaint in good faith to person having lawful authority may not amount to defamation
legal_provisions: Tort law distinction between Libel and Slander
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: In libel, the defamatory statement is in permanent and visible form (written words, pictures, etc.). In slander, it is in transitory form (spoken words, gestures). Since the complaint was in written form submitted to the Deputy Commissioner, it amounts to LIBEL defamation. Alternate answer: The 8th exception to Section 499 IPC states it is not defamation to prefer a good faith accusation to persons with lawful authority over the accused, so the complaint may not lead to defamation.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Correctly distinguishes libel vs slander AND correctly identifies complaint as libel OR correctly applies 8th exception
evaluation_criteria.good: Correctly identifies libel with definition but misses alternate argument
evaluation_criteria.partial: Confuses libel and slander or gives incomplete explanation
evaluation_criteria.minimal: Only names libel or slander without explanation

sub_questions.question_text: What is the jurisdiction of the Court to try civil suit 'where wrong done to the person'?

key_points: Section 19 of Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) 1908 governs this
Applies to suits for compensation for wrong done to person OR movable property
If wrong was done within jurisdiction of one Court AND defendant resides/carries on business/personally works for gain within jurisdiction of another Court
The suit may be instituted at the OPTION OF THE PLAINTIFF in either of the said Courts
Plaintiff has the choice between the two courts
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Under Section 19 CPC, where a suit is for compensation for wrong done to the person or movable property, if the wrong was done within the jurisdiction of one Court and the defendant resides or carries on business or personally works for gain within the jurisdiction of another Court, the suit may be instituted at the OPTION OF THE PLAINTIFF in either of the said Courts.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites Section 19 CPC with correct explanation of plaintiff's option
evaluation_criteria.good: Explains concept correctly without section reference
evaluation_criteria.partial: Mentions choice of court but misses the 'wrong done in one place, defendant residing in another' element

sub_questions.question_text: What is 'publication of defamatory words'?

key_points: Publication means making the defamatory matter known to some person OTHER THAN the person of whom it is written
The ambit of 'publish' is very wide
Publication is communication of the statement to any THIRD PARTY (not the claimant or defendant)
Even writing a defamatory statement to one person about another constitutes publication
The key requirement is that it must reach at least one other person besides the subject
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Publication of defamatory words means making known the defamatory matter to some person OTHER THAN the person of whom it is written. Publication is communication of the defamatory statement to any THIRD PARTY (i.e., not the claimant or the defendant). The ambit of 'publish' is very wide.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Clearly states communication to third party, explains it must reach someone other than subject
evaluation_criteria.good: Correct definition with most elements
evaluation_criteria.partial: Vague explanation about making it public

sub_questions.question_text: What is the time period of limitation for compensation in defamation?

key_points: For LIBEL: One year from when the libel is published
For SLANDER (actionable per se): One year when the words are spoken
For SLANDER (not actionable in themselves): One year when the special damage complained of results
These are under the Limitation Act
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Limitation for compensation in defamation: For Libel – 1 year from date of publication. For Slander – 1 year from when the words are spoken, or if words are not actionable in themselves, 1 year from when the special damage complained of results.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: States both libel and slander limitation periods with correct distinction
evaluation_criteria.good: States one year limitation with partial distinction between libel and slander
evaluation_criteria.partial: Only mentions one year without distinguishing between libel and slander
evaluation_criteria.minimal: Vague mention of a time period

questions.topic: Judicial Precedents, Transfer of Property, Contracts, Negotiable Instruments

sub_questions.question_text: What do you mean by Judicial Precedents? Determine and explain the kind of precedent in: (i) Vishaka guidelines (ii) Decision of one High Court on another High Court

key_points: Judicial Precedent: Guidance or authority of past decisions of courts for future cases. Only decisions laying down a NEW RULE OR PRINCIPLE are called judicial precedents

Part (i) Vishaka guidelines – ORIGINAL PRECEDENT: Created and applied a new rule of law regarding prevention of sexual harassment at workplace. It was law for future cases from 1997-2013 until POSH Act 2013 was enacted

Part (ii) Decision of one HC on another HC – PERSUASIVE PRECEDENT: A persuasive precedent is one which judges are NOT OBLIGED to follow but which they will take into consideration and attach great weight. Decision of one High Court may not be binding on another High Court but can give a principle which may be helpful (persuasive value)
legal_provisions: Case: Vishaka and Others v. State of Rajasthan (1997 SC)
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Judicial Precedent means the guidance or authority of past decisions of courts for future cases. Only decisions laying down a new rule or principle are judicial precedents. (i) Vishaka case = ORIGINAL PRECEDENT (created a completely new rule of law). (ii) HC decisions on other HCs = PERSUASIVE PRECEDENT (not binding but taken into consideration).

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Correct definition of judicial precedent + correctly identifies Original and Persuasive precedent with explanation
evaluation_criteria.good: Correct identification of both types with partial explanation
evaluation_criteria.partial: Identifies one type correctly
evaluation_criteria.minimal: Defines precedent but cannot classify types

sub_questions.question_text: Ramjilal made two gifts to Gajendra – one immovable property in Delhi (unregistered gift deed) and three movable properties (unregistered). Ramjilal died. Is Gajendra entitled to both gifts?

key_points: Gift of IMMOVABLE property: Compulsorily registerable under Registration Act 1908
Privy Council in Kalyana Sundram v. Karuppa AIR 1927 PC 42: If instrument of gift has been handed over by donor to donee and accepted, donor has done everything to complete donation
Death of donor is NOT a ground for refusing registration; the donee can present for registration after donor's death
Once registered, the gift deed operates from the date of EXECUTION
Gift of MOVABLE property: Registration is OPTIONAL, NOT compulsory under Registration Act 1908

Conclusion: Three movable property gifts to Gajendra are FULLY ENFORCEABLE without registration. The immovable property gift deed needs to be presented for registration; if registered, it will be valid from the date of execution
legal_provisions: Kalyana Sundram v. Karuppa AIR 1927 PC 42
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Immovable property gifts must be compulsorily registered. However, the donor's death does not bar registration. Gajendra can still get the gift deed registered; once registered it operates from date of execution. Movable property gifts are fully enforceable without registration as it is optional.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Correctly distinguishes movable vs immovable + explains death not being a bar to registration + cites Kalyana Sundram case
evaluation_criteria.good: Correct distinction between movable and immovable but misses death-not-a-bar point
evaluation_criteria.partial: Knows immovable must be registered but misses the rest

sub_questions.question_text: A, the son of B sold the property of B presuming that he will get the property of B after the death of B. Is it valid?

key_points: Section 6(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
The chance of an heir-apparent succeeding to an estate CANNOT be transferred
Also: the chance of a relation obtaining a legacy on the death of a kinsman or any other mere possibility of a like nature cannot be transferred
A cannot sell B's property as it is mere chance of an heir-apparent succeeding to an estate
Such a transfer is void
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Under Section 6(a) of TPA 1882, the chance of an heir-apparent succeeding to an estate cannot be transferred. Since A has only a mere expectancy/possibility of inheriting B's property, A cannot validly sell it. The transfer is void.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites Section 6(a) TPA and correctly identifies this as heir-apparent's chance which cannot be transferred
evaluation_criteria.good: Correct conclusion with correct reasoning without section citation
evaluation_criteria.partial: Says transfer is void but gives incomplete reason

sub_questions.question_text: Raiz draws a cheque of ₹50,000 on account having ₹49,000. Cheque bounces (S.138 NI Act). Can this be referred for amicable settlement through mediation?

key_points: Dayawati vs. Yogesh Kumar Gosain (Delhi HC, 2017): Key case on this issue
Though no express statutory provision enabling criminal court to refer S.138 matters to ADR, CrPC permits and recognises settlement
No bar to utilising ADR including arbitration, mediation, conciliation (recognised under Section 89 CPC) for settling disputes covered under Section 320 CrPC
Conclusion: YES, the matter CAN be referred for amicable settlement through mediation
legal_provisions: Dayawati v. Yogesh Kumar Gosain (Delhi HC 2017)
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: As held in Dayawati v. Yogesh Kumar Gosain (2017, Delhi HC), although no express provision enables criminal courts to refer S.138 NI Act cases to ADR, CrPC does permit settlement without restricting the process. There is no bar to using ADR (mediation, conciliation, arbitration) for settling disputes that are subject matter of offences under Section 320 CrPC. Hence, this matter CAN be referred for mediation.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites Dayawati case + explains the reasoning from CrPC + correct conclusion
evaluation_criteria.good: Correct conclusion with ADR/mediation reference even without case citation
evaluation_criteria.partial: Knows mediation is possible but cannot explain why

questions.topic: Sale of Goods, Contract Act – Fraud, Vicarious Liability

sub_questions.question_text: A sells 2 tons of oil to B. One ton by road (delivered), one ton by ship (in transit). B becomes insolvent before ship delivery. A stops goods in transit. Official Receiver claims goods. Will Official Receiver succeed?

key_points: Right of stoppage in transit under Sale of Goods Act, 1930
Right can be exercised when: (1) buyer becomes insolvent AND (2) goods are in transit
Buyer is insolvent if he has ceased to pay debts in ordinary course or cannot pay debts as due – need not be declared insolvent by court
Goods are in transit from time delivered to carrier until buyer takes delivery
Right exercised by taking actual possession OR giving notice to carrier
B is insolvent; goods are still in transit (on ship)
A CAN stop goods in transit; Official Receiver will NOT succeed
legal_provisions: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 – Right of Stoppage in Transit
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: A has the right of stoppage in transit as B is insolvent and goods are still in transit (on ship). This right can be exercised by taking actual possession or giving notice to the carrier. The Official Receiver will NOT succeed as A validly exercises this right.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Explains both conditions (insolvency + in transit) + correct conclusion that Official Receiver fails
evaluation_criteria.good: Correct conclusion with partial legal reasoning
evaluation_criteria.partial: Knows A can stop goods but cannot explain conditions

sub_questions.question_text: Can A resell the undelivered one ton of oil?

key_points: Section 54(2) Sale of Goods Act 1930: Where goods are perishable OR where unpaid seller exercising right of lien/stoppage gives NOTICE to buyer of intention to re-sell
If buyer does not pay within reasonable time after notice, seller may re-sell goods within reasonable time
Seller can recover from original buyer damages for any loss but buyer shall NOT be entitled to any profit on re-sale

Section 54(4): Where seller expressly reserves a right of re-sale in case of buyer's default, on buyer defaulting and seller re-selling, original contract of sale is rescinded (without prejudice to damages claim)
Conclusion: A CAN resell the undelivered one ton of oil in accordance with these provisions
legal_provisions: Section 54(2) and 54(4), Sale of Goods Act, 1930
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Under Section 54(2) and 54(4) of Sale of Goods Act 1930, A can resell the goods after exercising the right of stoppage in transit. A must give notice to the buyer of intention to resell. A can recover damages but buyer is not entitled to any profit on re-sale.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites Section 54(2)/(4) with notice requirement and profit allocation
evaluation_criteria.good: Correct conclusion that A can resell with some legal basis
evaluation_criteria.partial: Yes A can resell but incomplete reasoning

sub_questions.question_text: Brju (no license) induces Tarun (has license to buy) to contract for explosive chemical. Tarun pays ₹50,000 earnest money. Brju promises to get license but fails. Can Tarun recover advance payment?

key_points: Section 17 Indian Contract Act 1872 defines Fraud: Untrue statement made knowingly with intent to deceive

Key ingredients of fraud: false representation of fact, made with intent to be acted upon, actually induced other party, party deceived must be damaged, statement made knowing it was false or recklessly
Brju's representation that he had a license = fraud
Contract is VOIDABLE on account of fraud
Tarun can rescind/cancel/avoid the contract and recover advance paid
Tarun has right to claim compensation for damages sustained through non-fulfilment

ALTERNATE ANSWER: After knowing of fraud, Tarun agreed to continue when Brju promised to get license = Tarun did not reject the contract. The continued agreement is for an ILLEGAL purpose (trading explosive chemical without license). Illegal agreements are not enforceable at law. Hence Tarun CANNOT recover the advance
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Primary answer: Brju committed fraud under Section 17 ICA. The contract is voidable. Tarun can rescind and recover ₹50,000 + damages. Alternate answer: Once Tarun continued after discovering fraud (accepted Brju's promise to get license), the agreement became illegal (no license exists). Illegal agreements are void and unenforceable, so Tarun cannot recover the advance.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Identifies fraud under S.17 ICA + voidable contract + correct conclusion + mentions alternate answer
evaluation_criteria.good: Identifies fraud, voidable contract, and one correct conclusion
evaluation_criteria.partial: Knows it involves fraud but unclear on remedy

sub_questions.question_text: Bank security guard fires and kills John (a customer entering the bank). Bank argues it did not give permission to fire. Is bank vicariously liable?

key_points: Vicarious liability based on two maxims: (1) 'Qui facit per alium facit per se' – one who acts through another is deemed to do it himself; (2) 'Respondeat superior' – let the principal be liable
Master is liable for acts of servant done IN COURSE OF EMPLOYMENT
Act is in course of employment if: (a) master directly authorised the act OR (b) act done is an authorised act done WRONGLY
Wrong doing of an authorised act makes master liable
Cash box was being brought in; security guard's duty was to protect bank property
Guard's error in perceiving John as a threat was while performing authorised duty of protection
Act was in course of employment → Bank IS vicariously liable
Bank's defence that it did not give permission to fire is NOT acceptable
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Vicarious liability applies here. The two maxims (Qui facit per alium facit per se; Respondeat superior) make the master (bank) liable for the servant's (guard's) acts in course of employment. Protecting bank property/cash box is an authorised duty. The guard committed a wrong while performing this authorised duty. The bank cannot escape liability by saying it did not authorise the shooting – an authorised act done wrongly still makes the master liable.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Explains both Latin maxims + 'authorised act done wrongly' principle + correctly holds bank liable
evaluation_criteria.good: Correctly applies course of employment test and finds bank liable with some legal reasoning
evaluation_criteria.partial: Reaches correct conclusion but incomplete reasoning

questions.topic: Limitation Act, IT Act, Bail – OR – Arbitration, e-Stamping, Digital vs Electronic Signature

sub_questions.question_text: Akash (minor, age 13) when limitation period commenced. Cannot file suit due to disability. Can he file suit on cessation of minority? Limitation Act 1963.

key_points: Section 6 of Limitation Act 1963: Enabling section for persons under disability to exercise legal rights
Section 7 supplements Section 6; Section 8 controls both as exception
Disability includes minority
Under Section 6, a person under disability may file suit within maximum 3 years after cessation of disability/minority even if main limitation period has expired
This 3 years is counted from date of CESSATION of disability (not from date of attaining majority strictly)
Exception: Does not apply to suits for enforcement of rights of pre-emption
Conclusion: YES, Akash CAN file suit on cessation of minority (within 3 years from cessation)
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Section 6 of Limitation Act 1963 enables persons under disability (including minors) to file suits within 3 years after cessation of disability even after the general limitation period has expired. Akash can file suit within 3 years from when he ceases to be a minor. Exception: rights of pre-emption are excluded.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites Sections 6, 7, 8 + 3 year period from cessation + exception for pre-emption
evaluation_criteria.good: Cites Section 6 + correct conclusion + 3 year period
evaluation_criteria.partial: Knows Akash can file suit but cannot specify the period

sub_questions.question_text: Does Section 79 of IT Act 2000 (as originally enacted) deal with effect of other laws? [Google India Private Ltd. v. Vishaka Industries 2019 SC]

key_points: Section 79(1) IT Act 2000: Intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by him
Section 79(2)(c): Provisions apply if intermediary observes due diligence while discharging duties
Google India Private Limited v. Visakha Industries (SC 2019): Supreme Court decided that Section 79 as ORIGINALLY ENACTED did not deal with the effect of OTHER LAWS

High Court finding that Google did not block defamatory material despite notice – flawed on two counts: (1) S.79 as originally enacted had nothing to do with offences under other laws; (2) Defamation is under Section 499 IPC, and S.79 as originally enacted did not deal with effect of other laws
Conclusion: Section 79 of IT Act 2000 as ORIGINALLY ENACTED does NOT deal with effect of other laws
legal_provisions: Google India Private Limited v. Visakha Industries (SC, 10.12.2019)
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: The Supreme Court in Google India v. Visakha Industries (2019) held that Section 79 of the IT Act as originally enacted did NOT deal with the effect of other laws. Since defamation is an offence under Section 499 IPC (another law), Section 79 as originally enacted had nothing to do with freeing the intermediary from liability under IPC.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites Section 79 + Google India case + correct conclusion that it does NOT deal with other laws
evaluation_criteria.good: Correct conclusion with reference to case or section
evaluation_criteria.partial: Partially explains Section 79 but misses the specific SC finding

sub_questions.question_text: Is right to bail on touchstone of Article 21? State directions issued in Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022 SC).

key_points: SC held: 'Bail is the Rule and Jail is the Exception' – on the touchstone of Article 21 of Constitution of India
YES, right to bail is on touchstone of Article 21
Key directions (up to 12 listed in judgment):
1. Government may consider introducing a separate Bail Act
2. Investigating agencies must comply with Sections 41 and 41A CrPC; dereliction to be reported to higher authorities
3. Courts must satisfy themselves on compliance of S.41 and 41A; non-compliance = entitlement to bail
4. All State Governments/UTs to facilitate standing orders for S.41 and 41A procedure
5. No insistence on bail application while considering applications under Sections 88, 170, 204, 209 CrPC
6. Strict compliance with Siddharth judgment mandate
7. State/Central Governments to comply with directions on constitution of special courts; vacancies to be filled
8. High Courts to find undertrial prisoners unable to comply with bail conditions and take action under S.440
9. Mandate of S.440 on sureties to be kept in mind
10. Exercise to comply with S.436A at district and HC level
11. Bail applications to be disposed within 2 weeks; anticipatory bail applications within 6 weeks
12. All State Governments, UTs and HCs to file affidavits/status reports within 4 months
legal_provisions: Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI and Ors (SC, 11.07.2022)
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: YES, the right to bail is on the touchstone of Article 21 as held in Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022). 'Bail is the Rule, Jail is the Exception.' The Supreme Court issued 12 major directions covering: separate Bail Act, compliance with S.41/41A, disposal timelines (2 weeks for bail, 6 weeks for anticipatory bail), exercise under S.436A, special courts, undertrial prisoners' review, and status reports by governments.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Confirms Article 21 touchstone + lists at least 6-8 directions correctly
evaluation_criteria.good: Article 21 confirmed + 4-5 directions
evaluation_criteria.partial: Article 21 correct + 2-3 directions
evaluation_criteria.minimal: Only says bail is Rule, Jail is Exception without directions

questions.topic: Arbitration Award, e-Stamping, Digital vs Electronic Signature (Alternate to Q.4)

sub_questions.question_text: Explain the grounds for setting aside of an Arbitral Award under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

key_points: Section 34 of Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996

Section 34(2)(a) – Party-based grounds: (i) party under incapacity; (ii) arbitration agreement invalid; (iii) party not given proper notice of arbitrator appointment or proceedings, or otherwise unable to present case; (iv) award deals with dispute not contemplated by submission to arbitration or beyond scope; (v) composition of tribunal or procedure not in accordance with parties' agreement
Section 34(2)(b) – Court's own finding: (i) subject matter not capable of settlement by arbitration under law; (ii) award conflicts with PUBLIC POLICY OF INDIA

Explanation 1 to S.34: Award conflicts with public policy if: (i) induced/affected by fraud or corruption or violates S.75/S.81; (ii) contravenes fundamental policy of Indian law; (iii) conflicts with most basic notions of morality or justice
Explanation 2: Test of contravention with fundamental policy shall NOT entail review on merits

Section 34(2A): For domestic arbitrations (not international commercial), award may also be set aside if vitiated by PATENT ILLEGALITY appearing on face of award (not mere erroneous application of law)
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Section 34 provides grounds to set aside arbitral awards. S.34(2)(a): party-based grounds (incapacity, invalid agreement, no notice, beyond scope, improper composition). S.34(2)(b): court findings (non-arbitrable subject matter, conflict with public policy). Public policy includes fraud/corruption, violation of fundamental policy of Indian law, or conflict with basic morality/justice. S.34(2A): patent illegality for domestic arbitrations.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Covers all grounds under S.34(2)(a), S.34(2)(b), public policy explanation, and S.34(2A)
evaluation_criteria.good: Covers main grounds under S.34(2)(a) and (b) with public policy
evaluation_criteria.partial: Lists some grounds without full coverage

sub_questions.question_text: Explain the concept and verification of e-stamping.

key_points: E-stamping is a computer-based application and secure electronic way of stamping documents
Replaces physical stamp paper/franking system
Introduced in 2013 to reduce counterfeits and errors
Stock Holding Corporation of India Limited (SHCIL) is the Central Record Keeping Agency (CRA)
Verification: Can be verified ONLINE at www.shcilestamp.com

Steps to verify: Click 'Verify e-Stamp Certificate' and enter: (1) State, (2) Certificate Number (UIN – Unique Identification Number), (3) Stamp Duty Type / Description of Document, (4) Certificate Issue Date, (5) 6-character alphanumeric string
UIN is a unique system-generated number mentioned on the e-Stamp Certificate
Anyone with the UIN can check authenticity of the Certificate
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: E-stamping is a secure, computer-based alternative to physical stamp paper/franking, introduced in 2013. SHCIL is the CRA. Verification is done online at www.shcilestamp.com by entering the State, UIN (Certificate Number), Stamp Duty Type, Issue Date, and a 6-character alphanumeric string.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Explains concept + SHCIL as CRA + all 5 verification steps
evaluation_criteria.good: Explains concept + SHCIL + partial verification steps
evaluation_criteria.partial: Only explains concept without verification process

sub_questions.question_text: Is Digital Signature considered the same as Electronic Signature under the IT Act 2000? Discuss.

key_points: They are NOT the same – distinct concepts under IT Act 2000
Electronic Signature: Section 2(1)(ta) IT Act – wider concept; a digital form of a web link signature that is legally binding and secure
Digital Signature: Section 2(1)(p) IT Act – a secured signature that works with electronic signature and relies on public key infrastructure

Key differences: Purpose (verification vs securing a document), Validation (electronic – no trusted certificate authority required; digital – validated by trusted CA/TSP), Security (electronic – less secure, vulnerable to tampering; digital – highly secure), Verification (electronic – cannot be verified; digital – can be verified), Types (electronic – verbal, electronic ticks, scanned signatures; digital – Adobe, Microsoft), Utility (electronic – simpler but less evidential value; digital – preferred for authenticity)
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Digital Signature (S.2(1)(p)) and Electronic Signature (S.2(1)(ta)) are DIFFERENT under the IT Act 2000. Digital signature relies on public key infrastructure, is validated by trusted CAs, is highly secure, and can be verified. Electronic signature is a broader concept, includes ticks, scanned signatures, verbal forms, is less secure, cannot be independently verified, and has less evidential value.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites both sections + provides at least 4 distinctions with explanation
evaluation_criteria.good: Correctly states they are different + 3 distinctions
evaluation_criteria.partial: States they are different but only 1-2 distinctions
evaluation_criteria.minimal: Only says they are different without explanation

questions.topic: RTI Act, Conciliation, Civil Procedure Code

sub_questions.question_text: Right to Information Act 2005 – manner in which requests may be made by a citizen to the authority.

key_points: Section 6 of RTI Act 2005
Request must be in WRITING or through ELECTRONIC MEANS
Can be in English, Hindi, or OFFICIAL LANGUAGE of the area
Must be accompanied by PRESCRIBED FEE

Can be made to: (a) Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer of concerned public authority; OR (b) Central Assistant Public Information Officer or State Assistant Public Information Officer
Must specify particulars of information sought
If request cannot be made in writing: CPIO/SPIO shall render ALL REASONABLE ASSISTANCE to person making request orally to reduce same in writing
Applicant NOT REQUIRED to give reason for requesting information or any other personal details except those necessary for contacting him
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Under Section 6 RTI Act, citizens can make requests in writing or electronically in English/Hindi/official language with prescribed fee to the CPIO/SPIO or Assistant PIO. Oral requests must be assisted by PIO to be reduced to writing. No reason needs to be given for requesting information.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Covers: writing/electronic mode, languages, fee, officers to whom request is made, no reason required, oral assistance
evaluation_criteria.good: Covers 4-5 of the above elements
evaluation_criteria.partial: Covers 2-3 elements

sub_questions.question_text: Procedure for commencement of conciliation proceedings under Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996. How many conciliators can be there?

key_points: Section 62(1): Party initiating conciliation sends WRITTEN INVITATION to other party briefly identifying subject of dispute
Section 62(2): Conciliation commences when other party ACCEPTS IN WRITING the invitation
Section 62(3): If other party REJECTS invitation – NO conciliation proceedings
Section 62(4): If no reply within 30 DAYS from date of invitation (or other specified period) – initiating party may treat this as REJECTION, and must inform other party in writing of this election
Number of Conciliators – Section 63: Shall be ONE conciliator UNLESS parties agree to two or more
Where more than one conciliator: they ought, as a general rule, to ACT JOINTLY
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Conciliation commences with a written invitation (S.62(1)) → acceptance in writing (S.62(2)). Rejection ends proceedings (S.62(3)). Non-reply within 30 days = deemed rejection, initiating party must inform other party (S.62(4)). Number of conciliators: minimum 1, parties can agree on more; multiple conciliators must act jointly (S.63).

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Covers all four sub-sections of S.62 + S.63 on number of conciliators
evaluation_criteria.good: Covers main procedure (invitation, acceptance, rejection) + S.63
evaluation_criteria.partial: Covers invitation and acceptance only

sub_questions.question_text: Can a case triable by Special Judge under Criminal Law Amendment Act 1952 be transferred to High Court? [A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak 1988 SC]

key_points: A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak (SC 1988) AIR 1531
Court by its DIRECTIONS CANNOT CONFER JURISDICTION on a court that does not possess such jurisdiction
Power to CREATE or ENLARGE jurisdiction is LEGISLATIVE in character
Parliament alone can confer jurisdiction by law
No court – superior or inferior or both combined – can enlarge jurisdiction of a court or divest a person of rights of revision and appeal
Conclusion: A case triable by Special Judge CANNOT be transferred to High Court to try by itself if High Court does not have jurisdiction to try it
legal_provisions: A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak (SC, 29.04.1988) AIR 1988: 1531
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: As held in A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak (1988 SC), a court cannot by its directions confer jurisdiction it does not possess. Power to create or enlarge jurisdiction is legislative. Parliament alone can do this. Hence a case triable by Special Judge cannot be transferred to High Court if HC does not have jurisdiction to try it.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites Antulay case + explains legislative character of jurisdiction + correct conclusion
evaluation_criteria.good: Correct conclusion with correct principle even without case citation
evaluation_criteria.partial: Knows transfer is not possible but incomplete reasoning

sub_questions.question_text: Discuss the jurisdiction of Courts depending upon their powers.

key_points: Original Jurisdiction: Court tries and decides suits filed before it
Appellate Jurisdiction: Court hears appeals against decisions/decrees passed by subordinate courts
Criminal and Appellate Jurisdiction: SC, HCs, and District Courts have both original and appellate jurisdictions in various matters
Territorial jurisdiction: Fixed by Government for each court
Pecuniary jurisdiction: Section 6 CPC
Section 9 CPC: Courts shall have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature EXCEPT suits of which cognisance is expressly or impliedly barred
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Courts have: (1) Original Jurisdiction (try cases directly), (2) Appellate Jurisdiction (hear appeals from lower courts), (3) Both original and appellate (SC, HCs, District Courts). Territorial limits fixed by Government. Pecuniary jurisdiction under S.6 CPC. S.9 CPC: courts try all civil suits unless expressly/impliedly barred.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Covers original, appellate, S.6 CPC, S.9 CPC
evaluation_criteria.good: Covers at least original, appellate, and one CPC provision
evaluation_criteria.partial: Only explains original and appellate

questions.topic: Specific Performance, Indian Evidence Act, Stamp Act, Contract Act – OR – Statutory Interpretation, Administrative Law, Custom, Set-Off
questions.note: Students must attempt ALL parts of either Q.6 OR Q.6A (alternate)

sub_questions.question_text: Abhinav contracts to paint Manoj's house in a month and not take other painting jobs. Abhinav breaches. Manoj seeks specific performance. Will Manoj succeed? Distinguish injunction vs specific performance.

key_points: Section 14 Specific Relief Act 1963: Contract dependent on personal qualifications of parties or involving continuous duty that court cannot supervise CANNOT be specifically enforced
Painting contract = contract of PERSONAL NATURE depending on Abhinav's personal qualification
Manoj will NOT succeed in seeking specific performance of the painting (positive stipulation)
BUT: Negative stipulation (not to take other painting jobs) CAN be enforced by INJUNCTION

Distinction – Specific Performance vs Injunction: SP is for active duty (positive); Injunction prevents violation of negative duty. SP deals primarily with contracts; Injunction also covers torts. SP for trust enforcement; Injunction as preventive relief. Positive contract = SP; Negative contract = Injunction
legal_provisions: Sections on Injunction, Specific Relief Act, 1963
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Manoj will NOT succeed for specific performance as painting is a personal contract (S.14 SRA). However, the negative stipulation (not to work elsewhere) CAN be enforced by way of INJUNCTION. Specific Performance compels performance of positive duty; Injunction prevents breach of negative duty.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites S.14 SRA + NO for SP + YES for injunction on negative stipulation + clear distinction table/explanation
evaluation_criteria.good: S.14 cited + correct result on SP + injunction point
evaluation_criteria.partial: Correct result on SP but misses injunction/negative stipulation
evaluation_criteria.minimal: Vague answer about contracts being personal

sub_questions.question_text: A says to B about horse 'Go and ask C, C knows all about it.' C says 'Horse is sound.' Is C's statement confession or admission?

key_points: Section 17 Indian Evidence Act 1872: Admission is a statement (oral/documentary/electronic) suggesting inference as to any fact in issue or relevant fact
Section 20 IEA: Statements made by persons to whom a party to the suit has EXPRESSLY REFERRED for information in reference to a matter in dispute are ADMISSIONS
Illustration to S.20 exactly matches this fact: 'A says to B – Go and ask C, C knows all about it. C's statement is an admission.'
C's statement is an ADMISSION (not confession – confession applies to criminal cases by the accused)
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: C's statement is an ADMISSION under Section 20 of the Indian Evidence Act. When A expressly referred B to C for information, C becomes a person to whom the party referred – C's statement becomes admissible as admission against A.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites S.20 IEA with illustration + correctly identifies it as ADMISSION
evaluation_criteria.good: Correctly identifies it as Admission with S.20 reference
evaluation_criteria.partial: Correctly identifies as admission without legal basis

sub_questions.question_text: A confesses murder to wife. Wife summoned as witness against husband. Can A's wife act as witness?

key_points: Section 122, Indian Evidence Act, 1872
No person who is or has been married shall be COMPELLED to disclose any communication made to them during marriage by their spouse
Such person shall NOT BE PERMITTED to disclose such communication UNLESS the person who made it (or their representative in interest) CONSENTS
Exception: In suits between married persons, or proceedings where one married person is prosecuted for crime committed against the OTHER married person
Conclusion: A's wife CANNOT act as witness UNLESS A (who made the communication) or his representative in interest CONSENTS
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Under Section 122 IEA, communications between spouses during marriage are protected. A's wife cannot testify about his confession unless A himself consents. The marital privilege protects such confidential communications.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites S.122 IEA + correctly concludes wife cannot testify without A's consent
evaluation_criteria.good: Correct conclusion with S.122 reference
evaluation_criteria.partial: Correct conclusion without legal basis

sub_questions.question_text: Promissory note executed by Raja and Suraj; stamp affixed and cancelled by Raja by again signing AFTER execution. Are provisions of Indian Stamp Act 1899 complied with?

key_points: Section 17 of Indian Stamp Act 1899: All instruments chargeable with duty and executed by any person in India shall be STAMPED BEFORE OR AT THE TIME OF EXECUTION
Subsequent stamping (however close in time) cannot render the document as stamped at time of execution

Case: Rohini v. Fernandes AIR 1956 Bom 421: Where a promissory note is executed by 'A' and 'B' and stamp is AFTERWARDS affixed and cancelled by 'A' by again signing it, stamping has taken place SUBSEQUENT TO EXECUTION
Conclusion: Provisions of Section 17 of Indian Stamp Act 1899 are NOT COMPLIED WITH in this situation
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: Section 17 of the Indian Stamp Act requires stamping BEFORE OR AT THE TIME of execution. In this case, the stamp was affixed AFTER execution, which violates S.17. As held in Rohini v. Fernandes (AIR 1956 Bom), subsequent stamping does not cure the defect. Provisions are NOT complied with.

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites S.17 ISA + Rohini case + correct conclusion of non-compliance
evaluation_criteria.good: Cites S.17 + correct conclusion even without case citation
evaluation_criteria.partial: Mentions timing requirement but incomplete reasoning

sub_questions.question_text: Arun (husband) enters registered agreement with wife Radha to pay his earnings to her. Valid? What if husband by registered document (after referring to quarrels) promises to pay wife money for maintenance and separate residence?

key_points: Section 25 ICA: Agreement without consideration is void EXCEPT Section 25(1) – express in writing + registered + made on account of NATURAL LOVE AND AFFECTION between parties in near relation
Case 1: Poonoo Bibi v. FyazBuksh (1874 Bom): A registered agreement between husband and wife to pay his earnings to her IS VALID – in writing, registered, near relation, made for love and affection

Case 2: Rajluckhy Deb v. Bhootnath (1900): Husband by registered document after referring to QUARRELS AND DISAGREEMENT promised to pay wife for maintenance and separate residence – UNENFORCEABLE – NOT made for love and affection (quarrels indicate absence of affection)
Conclusion: First agreement = VALID. Second agreement = UNENFORCEABLE (no natural love and affection, as quarrels indicate)
legal_provisions: Poonoo Bibi v. FyazBuksh (1874) 15 Bom L.R. 57
expected_answer.full_answer_summary: S.25(1) ICA: Agreement without consideration valid if written + registered + natural love and affection + near relations. First case (Poonoo Bibi) = VALID (all conditions met). Second case (Rajluckhy Deb) = UNENFORCEABLE (quarrels and disagreement negate natural love and affection).

evaluation_criteria.full_marks: Cites S.25(1) + both cases + correct conclusions for both situations
evaluation_criteria.good: S.25(1) cited + correct conclusions for both with at least one case
evaluation_criteria.partial: Correct conclusion for first situation, incomplete on second
evaluation_criteria.minimal: Only general mention of consideration or valid/invalid without reasons
